summary.text: A 36-year-old woman with prior sicca symptoms and axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy under immunologic evaluation since 2020 presented to the Infectious Diseases Department with a three-day history of high-grade fever, profuse watery diarrhea, fatigue, myalgia and progressive proximal muscle weakness leaving her unable to walk unassisted, plus a 10 kg weight loss over the preceding month and increasing dysphagia. Examination showed a chronically ill, emaciated, dehydrated patient with hypotonia, muscle tenderness, reduced reflexes, reduced grip strength, distal sensorimotor deficits and livedo reticularis.

Initial laboratory results (Table 1) showed CPK above 42670 U/L, raised transaminases and LDH, hypokalemia, low calcium, anemia, leukocytosis, raised CRP and RF, and low C3 and C4. Urinalysis showed alkaline urine with proteinuria and urinary red cells. Immunoserology was strongly positive for SS-A and Ro-52 with positive PCNA and ANA. Electromyoneurography showed a myopathic pattern, and infectious causes were ruled out by microbiological testing.

Diagnoses were primary Sjögren syndrome overlapping with polymyositis, distal renal tubular acidosis with non-anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia, rhabdomyolysis, inflammatory myopathy and hypocomplementemia. She was started on continuous renal replacement therapy with concurrent CytoSorb hemoadsorption.

On day 5 she developed signs of an acute abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT showed free intraperitoneal air, pericolonic inflammation and bowel wall thickening. Emergency laparotomy found perforation of the descending colon and inflammatory gallbladder changes, treated with left hemicolectomy, terminal ileostomy, cholecystectomy and peritoneal lavage. Histology showed vasculitis-induced ischemic colitis with necrotizing vasculitis and gangrenous cholecystitis.

Postoperatively she was in the ICU on broad-spectrum antibiotics and parenteral nutrition. After surgical stabilization and histologic confirmation, she received intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide 800 mg with high-dose methylprednisolone tapering, intravenous hydration, Mesna and antiemetic prophylaxis, followed by gradual enteral nutrition and early physical rehabilitation for severe sarcopenia and muscle atrophy.

She improved clinically with normalization of electrolyte and laboratory parameters and functional recovery within two weeks, remained stable with improving abdominal symptoms, tolerated cyclophosphamide and continued maintenance immunosuppression. She was discharged home on hospital day 33 ambulatory with minimal assistance and enrolled in outpatient rehabilitation. At three months she was clinically stable without recurrent vasculitis, gastrointestinal complications or renal decline, under regular rheumatology and nephrology monitoring; elective stoma reversal is to be considered later.
